positions.commentary: The speaker uses Microsoft as an example of understanding how a company changes over time, noting the importance of understanding the trajectory from 2011 to 2016.
The speaker previously held a value investor mindset that Netflix was not worth its valuation, but later corrected this mistake and believes the company will benefit from industry shakeouts.
Dollar Tree has become a meaningful part of the speaker's portfolio, and he has followed the company for a decade, eventually acting on his positive thoughts regarding management and strategy.
Five Below is used as an example of a small retailer where the quality and confidence of the merchant team is really important to how the business does over time.

notes: Alex Morris, founder of TSOH Investment Research, shares his insights from Microsoft’s CEO Satya Nadella's book 'Hit Refresh.' We discuss the importance of empathy in leadership, cultural transformation, and finding your edge in equity research. Our conversation with Alex Morris was recorded on 16 June 2025. After four great years, this episode marks the last one with Niklas as co-host. Eddie will continue Investing by the Books podcast with the same steadfast ambition: to invite masterminds to discuss books that help us think, invest, and live better. For more info about the podcast, go to the episode page and make sure to follow us on X/Twitter . We love to hear your thoughts on what you like and what we can improve, so please give us your rating and a review. You’re also very welcome to tell us about great authors, books, and investors you want to hear on the show. Thank you! /Eddie & Niklas with team ————————————— Episode Chapters (00:00) Intro and Farewell to a Co-Host (01:45) Welcoming Alex Morris (04:06) Transitioning to ‘Hit Refresh’ (05:54) Satya Nadella as an Author (08:56) Satya Nadella's Leadership Style (10:53) Exploring the Concept of 'Hit Refresh' (15:38) The Significance of Succession in Leadership (17:30) Cultural Transformation in Microsoft (19:10) Incentivizing Change: Lessons from Nadella (21:57) Leadership Vision (23:22) Microsoft's Three Tech Bets (26:49) Researching Large Caps (29:33) The Science of Hitting (34:19) Fixed Mindset vs. Growth Mindset (Netflix Example) (37:35) Alex’ Investable Universe (41:05) Active Research Techniques (43:08) The Future of Equity Analysts (45:57) Buffett and Munger Unscripted (49:33) Exploring Other Book Ideas (51:21) Influential Figures in Investing (54:29) Concluding remarks ————————————— Books Mentioned Hit Refresh – Satya Nadella Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder Letters Lessons from the Titans – Carter Copeland, Rob Wertheimer, and Scott Davis Buffett and Munger Unscripted – Alex Morris The Essays of Warren Buffett – Lawrence Cunningham One Up on Wall Street – Peter Lynch My Father's Business – Cal Turner, Jr. One Buck at a Time – Macon Brock ————————————— Companies Mentioned Microsoft Amazon Disney Netflix Cava Chipotle Dollar Tree Five Below ————————————— More on Alex Morris Website: https://thescienceofhitting.com/ X: https://x.com/TSOH_Investing ————————————— About the Podcast Intro episode: https://www.redeye.se/podcast/investing-by-the-books/817383/0-intro-to-investing-by-the-books ————————————— What is Investing by the Books? Investing by the Books was founded by Henrik Andersson, Bo Börtemark, Mats Larsson and Michael Persson. How are you?
I'm good, but it's also a bit sad today as this will be my last episode for the podcast.

Thank you, Niklas.

Alex is also the author of Buffett and Munger Unscripted, which was released in January

But Niklas, which book will we speak about today?
So today we will speak about Hitre Fresh, which Alex selected, and it's written by Sachin
Adela, the current CEO of Microsoft, and the forward is written by the founder of Microsoft
Bill Gates.
Hitre Fresh was published in 2017, and we are thrilled to speak about the book today.
Here comes our conversation with Alex Morris.
Hi Alex, and welcome to investing by the books podcast.
Thanks for having me.
I'm excited for this one.
It's great to have you on.
We recently met in Omaha, where are we reaching you today?
I am down in South Florida, back from Omaha.
It was a fun time, as I was telling you guys before we started actually drove to Earth
my family, which includes a one-year-old.
It was our first time doing a long drive with a one-year-old, and I learned some important
lessons along the way.
And to begin, can you tell our listeners a bit about your background and what led you
into the world of investing?
Sure.
Well, I went to college in the mid-2000s, and I had no clue what I wanted to do basically.
My dad's a plumber over here in the southeast US, and I thought maybe I could do something
like that.
So I went into building construction at first, didn't take too long to realize that maybe
isn't what I wanted to do.
It doesn't help being down in South Florida.
It's very, very hot during the summers, and the weather in general is not good.
So I didn't really want to be outside all the time.
Around that time, I stumbled across the Berkshire shareholder letters, and I kind of became
hooked right away.
Actually, Buddy and I drove to Omaha, a year or so later, thankfully, we went to school
in Northern Florida as opposed to Southern Florida, so that knocked out about five hours
of the drive that time around.
When was that?
That was in, I believe, that was 2009, I believe, it's hard to remember.
But yeah, so that was more than 15 years ago now, and I feel like I've just been on a
long journey of trying to get smarter every day, and sometimes move more slowly at that
than I'd like.
But yeah, I got a job in the industry in 2011 as a Biosite equities analyst.
I've been writing online for a long time about investments, and that kind of led to in
2021, I left the industry and started TSO, which investment research, which is basically
an outsourced equities analyst with a hundred percent transparency for my subscribers.
So yeah, it's been a couple of years of that now, I kind of launched a fingers crossed,
hoping that a lot of the readers who have been with me over the prior decade would find
their way along, and thankfully, it's kind of worked out well, so it's been an enjoyable
experience.
We'll speak more about your business a little bit later, but no, we will begin with speaking
about Hit Refresh, a book that you said you wanted to speak about, and I mean, I guess
you read all the Buffett's book, Buffett books, so refreshing to do something else.
How did you, how did you first come across this book?
Yeah, I mean, it's funny, Microsoft is a company that is really instrumental to kind of my
evolution as an investor, and a lot of what I think I've learned, and also what has kind
of been reinforced in some ways over the course of the last, again, call it 15, 20 years.
When I really started saving a little bit of money coming out of college and started
investing, it was safe for real, Microsoft was one of the first companies I owned, and
at the time it was very much a traditional value investment approach to the stock, and
as we'll talk about today with the book, Sokchen Adele's hiring in early 2014, I'm sure
I didn't fully grasp this at the time, or even a couple of years down the road, but I
started to really appreciate the importance of management and culture, and a lot of other
things that are discussed in this book, and as it ties into the investment part of the
equation, it was also a really instructive learning experience in terms of, okay, this
thing was at 10 times X Cash a couple years ago, now it's at 15 times, or now it's
at 20 times, what does that mean, and how do you kind of adjust your thought process as
a business is truly changing, even one of this size, which is kind of amazing when you
think about it, and it speaks to I selected this book and why I think so highly of Sachin
Adele.
And Sachin Adele's, of course, the author of the book, I mean, I read many different types
of sort of biographies, written by current CEOs, and some of them are better than others,
so to speak, and what sort of, what do you think makes Sachin a good author?
Yeah, it's funny, I think that the way you just said it is, there are some, there are
some business books written by current CEOs who are going through, in this case, I think
he called it the hard process of renewal, just to put a time frame on this.
So Sachin became CEO in February 2014, I checked before we hopped on publication date with
September of 17, and obviously you can imagine it takes, or as I've learned in the last
couple years, it takes some time to write a book and to get it published and all that jazz,
so I heard him saying one interview, this is different in terms of, we're in the middle
of it right now, he's not, he's not 10 years past his retirement, reflecting back on what
went wrong and what didn't go right, or what went right, he was in the thick of it.
And stock prices and everything, but that's, I looked also in September 17 when this came
out, Microsoft stock was at $70, which, you know, today it's at $470, so some indication
that a lot has continued to change over time, and maybe even at that point in time, it wasn't
kind of fully recognized where the company is coming from and where they were going.
So that part of it is, for me, what makes the book most unique, and I'm sure we'll get
into this, but particularly around the company's server and tools business and the transition
that was going on in the industry to cloud computing, and then also Microsoft's own experience
with that transition. I pulled some numbers just before hopping on to get some context for
this part of the conversation. When we got numbers for Amazon web services a few years later,
which was kind of not kind of the leading player in cloud computing at that point in time,
as Microsoft's going through this in the 13, 14, 15 period. In Q1 of 16, AWS was at,
it had exceeded $10 billion in run rate now, but revenues, and a few years earlier,
it was, you know, this tiny cloud computing business, it's not that much of a threat,
that fast-forward 16, it's at more than $10 billion in run rate revenues.
Around that time, when Adelaide became CEO, Microsoft's server and tools business was
a $20 billion revenue stream. So obviously, $10 and $20 is starting to become more of a problem,
right? But on that $20 billion revenue, they generated $8 billion to be bit. So, you know,
again, as you're thinking about what's happening internally as this transition is happening,
those numbers kind of speak to the incentives that they had to kind of navigate around
and figure out. And the most instructed part of the book to me is Adela talking about
coming into server and tools and navigating that.
And before we dive deeper into those areas, I think it would be good if you could
describe a little bit more about Adela, who he is as a person and where he's coming from.
Yeah. I think in the introduction, Bill Gates writes this line kind of stuck with me.
Adelaide was humble, forward-looking, and pragmatic. It's a very concise way to describe
someone, but I think those three words or terms are kind of perfectly descriptive of who he is,
or at least my perception of who he is. If he continued, he raised smart questions about
his strategy and he worked well with the hardcore engineers. He immediately put his mark in the
company, but didn't completely break it. As a title implies, he hit refresh. I think all of that is
it's really important in terms of what he goes on to describe about the culture. And
what was the path to moving the company forward that would actually work?
He has a really, I mean, obviously he has, as you can see from his resume or credentials, he obviously

one point in the book, I think it's instructive of who he is, or his learning. He says,
I like to think that the CEO stands for culture. The CEO is the curator of the organization's culture.
And that's a lot of the framing that he has throughout the book. He's also had things

at times, it is not easily quantified, right? But it's massively, massively important in terms of
where it actually goes over five, 10, 20 years.
Definitely. And it's clear that Medella has a big passion for technology. And I like how he
describes in the book, this magical feeling, the first time you experience a profound new technology.
So I'm curious if you have any such magical tech memory.
Well, not really. It's funny. For Microsoft, how you've been such a large and important
position of me in my portfolio, from a technical perspective, I still struggle to keep up with
everything that's going on. I'm pretty, by business, I write it through substack, which takes
care of everything besides the research and the writing. And thankfully, they exist because if
they didn't, I would be, I'd be in a bad place. So maybe finding substack is my answer to that
question because I, yes, I would invest for research probably would not exist if there wasn't
something like that in the world. The name of the book is hit refreshing. You were touching a
little bit upon the meaning. But what do you think it means? And what's the purpose of having
that tactic for this book? Yeah, I think, you know, again, I think it's really coming from the
perspective of a cultural view of the company more so than a question of technical prowess or
obviously financial resources, anything along those lines. Microsoft was still in credit
of the well-position. You know, Adele writes in the book, our culture had been rigid.
Hierarchy and pecking order had taken control and spontating. Creativity had suffered as a result.
Success can cause people to learn the habits that made them successful in the first place.
And he references early in the book. This, this fame is kind of like cartoon drawing of the
different Microsoft organizations and it's basically just a hand with a gun pointing, he's pointing
at each other basically. And he talks about this particularly when you get into again the
discussion of the cloud computing transition. He says, the organization basically didn't disagree,
broadly speaking with the idea that this is where things were going. They would just say,
yeah, we should do this and incubate it, but also, but it's not forget. Again, the numbers I said
earlier, we have this business over here that that generates at the time, you know, $8 billion
of operating in come a year. So let's not let that just go by the wayside also, by the way,
have salespeople down the organization, et cetera, who are compensated based on the
success of that business, right? I think he came in, and as he says in the book, again, he was in
a separate division. And when he was moved to server and tools, I think it was around the time,
if I have this correct, Ray Ozzy was leading this effort on what became Azure over time.
It was co-named bread dog. And when Ray Ozzy left, he says, the one in in refutable truth is that
in any large organization, any transformation that is to stick must come from within.
And I think Adela does a really good job of saying I came into this business
around the time that this is happening. It's not really my business, right? There's people
who work in this business and who are trying to figure out how to go forward. And I could have
brought the team over with me that I had been working with and people I was familiar with.
But I didn't think that was the right way to do it because again, it has to come from within.
The server and tools team needs to be the one to figure out how to move forward.
And I need to be able to connect with them and show them a way for us to do this.
Again, this is as you take it back to the long-term results of the business and the long-term
results of the stock, this is a massively important part of what would play out at Microsoft over
the next 15 years and continues to this day. So it just makes me reflect and to think about
when you own a business, if you're truly going to own something long-term,
the one, how do you monitor these things or get a sense for them? But to the extent that you do,
when you have a lot of conviction in that view, how does it then inform
how you think about the outputs of the DCF or how it trades relative to peers or whatever it may be?
Those are difficult questions to answer, especially with any level of specificity.
But I think the answer you can comfortably lead towards is that
it doesn't deserve to trade at a few turns on a multiple relative to an average company, right?
And that's a really important lesson that I thank a lot of traditional value investors, especially
struggle at times to implement. Obviously, it always depends on the game you're playing at things
like that, but to be extent you're truly trying to think an act long-term. It's a really important
lesson in my view. And it's clear that succession is a big thing in companies and he's the third
CEO ever in Microsoft. And it was not very likely or he was not an expected CEO choice as well, right?
No, it was incredibly messy. That process, and it's been over a decade now, but I can remember at
that time names that were batted around, most notably Alan Malali, who was either the CEO,
the former CEO at Ford Motor Company, and he was, I believe it was in his late 60s.
And when Nadella was ultimately tapped after a pretty extended kind of public selection process,
a lot of the response, at least from kind of financial press, was he's an insider and the company
is not going to be able to change, which is funny to think about. He has since framed it as
being an insider was kind of a beneficial thing because I could point to the company and what
was wrong would need to be fixed and I wasn't pointing back at other people. I was pointing out
myself to some extent. Yeah, I can remember at that time, it's funny. I've tried to find this
so many times. There was a blog post written by an individual who had sold a business to Microsoft,
and Nadella's division was basically the, they were the ones that were acquiring this company.
And this individual wrote a blog where he said, basically, the things that are being said about
Sachin Nadella, completely, they completely underestimate who he is and what he can potentially do
in this role. And yeah, in hindsight, that gentleman was, I'm sure he was already quite wealthy
because he sold the business to Microsoft. If he bought some shares or how it's some shares as a
result of that conclusion, that has worked out well for him. Yeah, I mean, speaking about culture,
one of the best definitions that we have heard. And I think Nicholas agrees with me in Episode
53. We spoke about lessons from the Titans. Maybe you're familiar with this book, but they
really describe culture as an output and not an input. You can't say we're going to have this
culture and then it happens. Rather, it's an output of how management behaves and the incentives
you put in there. And I think Nadella is really like proving by going first and he's really
strong on, for example, empathy, which is quite unusual. How important do you think that has been
in the business? Yeah, I think hugely. I think to that point, he says that in terms of strategy,
but I think it's perfectly applicable to culture as well. He says something along the lines of
if the leadership team is an end-to-part on strategy, by the time it works, it's way down the
organization. You'll end up miles apart in terms of I think it's a very similar idea. He also
says things like, and it's a quote that he kind of took from the CEO of LinkedIn at the time of
the deal, but he says I think its consistency is trust basically. Again, a lot of these things are,
it's maybe it's similar to my love for Warren and Charlie. A lot of the things are pretty
straightforward and concepts that are not that difficult to grasp, but to do these things consistently
over a long period of time. And that part is more difficult than it appears, I guess, because there's
not too many companies or leaders that are like these people, at least in my view.
And what do you think we can learn from Nadella when it comes to incentivizing people in an organization?
Yeah, I think you need to, again, most notably in terms of what will happen at server-in-tools,
when you come in, and I think the Gates quote hits at this, right, in terms of didn't completely
break it, kind of refreshed it. You start by understanding where they're coming from and ensuring
that they're kind of along for the journey and can appreciate the changes that are underway.
And obviously, to the extent that you can alter incentives and compensation structures to align
with that, that's a particularly effective way to get people to see where you're trying to go.
Yeah, and again, I think the example of him coming over from the Bing team and not just bringing
his top five people and putting them into the most important roles and basically saying,
hey, you guys work for us, just do what we say. It's a really notable example of that same idea.
And it's very little in terms of sort of monetary incentives. I don't think Nadella speaks a lot
about sort of the monetary incentives. More that sort of people needs to feel that this is the
right place to be where I can really make a change and sort of inspiring them to do what they really
want and that sort of give them the freedom to do what they want inside Microsoft was quite clear.
Yeah, yeah, it's one of the main things he said in terms of the cultural stuff that we're talking
about for empowering people. Perhaps number one thing leaders have to do, bolster confidence of
people that you're leading and power them and it's a recurring thing that you hear and something
that, again, we can all understand as we stop and actually think about it. On the point of compensation
more generally, I think it's kind of something as it, for me, at least as an investor, something I
kind of evolved on a bit over time. Alignment is obviously very important and you can go through
proxies and read them and that is a valuable exercise. There also is, in my view, as I look at someone
like Sachin Nadella, again, these people are all incredibly wealthy, so that helps. But I look at
a Sachin Nadella, I look at a read hastings, people like them and I don't know, you just get a strong
sense after enough time and after reading a book like this that, sure, the financial stuff matters
but he's not overly driven by, I've confidence saying he's not overly driven by whether or not his
constructions going to pay out at 80% of target or 100% of target, he's trying to do it's right for
the company long term and typically that leads to the best outcome anyways on that compensation. But
again, if you can find people like that and they're pretty rare, you should treat that accordingly
in terms of how you rate that. Do you have any other lessons from Nadella when it comes to
his leadership style? Yeah, I mean, I think it's mostly the ones we've discussed here in terms of
real clarity of vision. I liked in his when he was first, when he first became CEO, he sent
an email to the organization where it had a really good job of, again, like, kind of clearly
stating his view of where they were trying to go and making that evident to the people throughout
the company. It's obviously a huge company, right? And he said, while we have seen great success,
we are hungry to do more. Our industry is not respect to tradition and only respects innovation.
It's a critical time for the industry and for Microsoft. Making a mistake, we are headed for
greater places as technology evolves and as we evolve with it. Our job is to ensure Microsoft
thrives in a mobile and cloud-first world. And again, like I think that he's hit on some of
these messages over and over and over again, whether it's in, you know, investor communications or
or the internal emails and things that eventually get leaked periodically. There's a real clarity of
where the company is trying to go and, you know, the things that they're trying to do to get it there.
And I think that's incredibly valuable as opposed to a lot of stop, start, type activity that you
could see at businesses, particularly public trading companies to say try to navigate earnings and
things like that. As you said before, the book was published in 2017 and Nadella talks about Microsoft's
three big bets, mixed reality AI and quantum computing. And it's not 2025. How have these bets
played out? Yeah, it's funny. That's one of the parts that, as I went back and reread it.
I'm appreciating now that this stuff was getting talked about a lot more even five plus years ago. And I,
again, maybe doing my lack of technical prowess. I just kind of went up at a little bit and I didn't
really pay too much attention. I mean, obviously, things have changed pretty immediately here in
the last couple of years. I think some of the things that he talks about, it still seems like Microsoft's
position in those markets is still either very early or they're not kind of leading that
move. There's other things like the section on AI where you step back and go again, he was probably
writing this in 15 or 16. And now you can look back with a decade of hindsight to kind of judge
where he thought things were going. And he had a pretty good idea of where things were going,
which is really impressive. And as we know subsequently from opening ideals and stuff like that.
So yeah, it's the part of the book that for me is it's still interesting, but it's not
it's really the front part of the book where he talks about his journey at Microsoft where I
I think there's really a ton of value. But yeah, some of some of the stuff in the back to the extent that
you can understand it is a pretty interesting too. He's he's a very smart guy.
And sort of if we go in a bit deeper, maybe into the first part of the book, do you have any
other lessons from there that you want to share? Yeah, I mean, I think
and again, they're all kind of related, right? This idea of transformation and change
at companies and how how it's dealt with and you know, how that really feels inside of an organization
and you know, from my from my perspective as an investor, I've seen it. I've seen it here in this
in this business to some extent. It was a little bit earlier in my career. So I was not as
seasoned, but I've now seen it also in the media business with you know, Disney Netflix and all
